title: A holistic overview of deep learning approach in medical imaging

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Medical Imaging Modalities
subsections.subsection_title: Deep Learning Foundations for Medical Imaging
subsections.content:
Deep learning in medical imaging builds on multilayer neural networks that learn hierarchical representations directly from data, progressively transforming pixels or voxels into task-relevant abstractions such as anatomy, pathology, and clinical risk. The modern resurgence of the field is commonly attributed to advances in representation learning, large-scale optimization, and computing, synthesized in broad overviews of deep learning and its impact across perception tasks ref [1]. For medical imaging, this hierarchy is especially attractive because handcrafted pipelines often struggle with the heterogeneity of acquisition physics, anatomy, and disease presentation.

A core foundation is gradient-based end-to-end learning via backpropagation, which enabled practical optimization of multilayer models and later became the default training mechanism for convolutional and related architectures ref [2]. Early constrained architectures for handwritten digit recognition demonstrated key principles that remain central in medical imaging: local receptive fields, weight sharing, subsampling, and the incorporation of domain structure to improve generalization under limited labeled data ref [2]. These ideas foreshadowed contemporary medical-image networks, where inductive biases are crucial for learning from high-dimensional images with relatively small curated cohorts.

Another foundational milestone was unsupervised layer-wise pretraining with deep belief nets, which addressed optimization difficulties in deep models and highlighted the value of learning latent structure before supervised fine-tuning ref [5]. Although large labeled datasets and improved optimizers have reduced reliance on such pretraining, its underlying motivation persists in medical imaging, where annotation is expensive and weakly labeled or unlabeled scans are abundant. Thus, the conceptual foundations of deep learning for medical imaging rest on three enduring elements: hierarchical feature learning ref [1], scalable gradient-based optimization ref [2], and representation learning from unlabeled data ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Medical Imaging Modalities
subsections.subsection_title: Medical Imaging Modalities and Clinical Context
subsections.content:
Medical imaging encompasses modalities with distinct physics, spatial and temporal resolution, contrast mechanisms, cost profiles, and safety constraints, all of which shape how deep learning methods should be designed and evaluated. Radiography and CT provide fast, high-throughput depiction of anatomy and acute pathology, but CT and nuclear imaging rely on ionizing radiation; large population studies have documented substantial growth in CT, MRI, ultrasound, and PET utilization, alongside increasing cumulative radiation exposure from advanced imaging, especially in older patients ref [4]. By contrast, MRI and ultrasound avoid ionizing radiation and are central when soft-tissue contrast, hemodynamics, or bedside accessibility is prioritized ref [4], ref [3].

Clinical context is equally important because the same anatomical target may be imaged for screening, triage, diagnosis, treatment planning, or longitudinal response assessment. Mammography emphasizes population screening and subtle lesion detection; chest radiography supports rapid frontline assessment; CT dominates trauma, oncology staging, and lung imaging; MRI is prominent in neuro, musculoskeletal, pelvic, and breast imaging; ultrasound is operator dependent but indispensable in obstetrics, cardiology, and point-of-care settings; and PET/SPECT provide functional and metabolic information often fused with CT or MRI ref [3]. In radiation oncology, imaging further extends to contouring, dose estimation, image guidance, and adaptive therapy workflows ref [3].

These modality-specific characteristics create different data regimes and failure modes for deep learning. CT and MRI are often volumetric and multiphase, ultrasound is noisy and vendor/operator sensitive, radiography compresses 3D anatomy into 2D projections, and PET is lower resolution but biologically informative. Accordingly, clinically useful models must account for acquisition heterogeneity, workflow integration, radiation risk where relevant, and task-specific endpoints rather than treating “medical imaging” as a single homogeneous domain ref [4], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Medical Imaging Modalities
subsections.content:
Canonical deep architectures for image analysis in medical imaging largely inherit their design principles from natural-image vision, while being adapted to dense prediction and data-scarce settings. VGG popularized the use of small stacked 3×3 convolutions to build deep, uniform feature hierarchies, offering strong transferability despite high computational cost ref [9]. Inception architectures instead pursued multi-scale processing with parallel branches and factorized convolutions, improving parameter efficiency and receptive-field diversity; later variants combined these ideas with stronger regularization and residual connections to further stabilize deep optimization ref [10], ref [6].

Residual learning became a central architectural advance because skip connections alleviate degradation in very deep networks and enable substantially deeper feature extractors without proportional optimization difficulty ref [7]. In medical imaging, ResNet-style backbones are now common for classification, detection, and as encoders within segmentation systems, especially when pretrained on large external datasets. Closely related fully convolutional formulations for dense prediction replaced fully connected layers with pixelwise outputs, establishing a template for semantic segmentation that strongly influenced medical image analysis pipelines ref [9].

For biomedical segmentation, U-Net is the canonical architecture. Its encoder-decoder design couples a contracting path for contextual abstraction with an expansive path for precise localization, while lateral skip connections fuse coarse semantic and fine spatial information ref [8]. This design directly addressed limited annotation regimes through efficient end-to-end training and aggressive augmentation, and it rapidly became the basis for many 2D and 3D derivatives, including volumetric extensions such as 3D U-Net ref [10] and encoder-decoder segmentation variants like SegNet ref [11]. More broadly, architecture choice in medical imaging is task dependent: compact classification backbones often derive from VGG, Inception, or ResNet families, whereas lesion, organ, and cell delineation still predominantly follows the U-Net paradigm ref [9], ref [10], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Medical Imaging Modalities
subsections.subsection_title: Representation Learning, Transfer Learning, and Learning Paradigms
subsections.content:
Representation learning is central in medical imaging because labels are scarce, expensive, and often task-specific. Beyond supervised end-to-end training, recent work has emphasized learning reusable priors from unlabeled scans through self-supervision and reconstruction-based pretext tasks. In 3D imaging, Models Genesis showed that generic autodidactic pretraining can substantially improve downstream classification, detection, and segmentation, particularly when volumetric annotations are limited [4]. More broadly, transfer learning provides the conceptual basis for reusing such representations across domains, tasks, and distributions, with fine-tuning depth and source-target relatedness strongly influencing outcomes [11].

In practice, transfer learning in medical imaging has followed two main routes: adaptation from large natural-image models and transfer across medical datasets. For computer-aided detection and classification, ImageNet initialization often improves optimization stability and performance relative to training from scratch, especially in limited-data regimes [12]. Systematic comparisons further showed that fine-tuning generally outperforms both fixed off-the-shelf features and full training, although the optimal strategy depends on training set size and task similarity [13]. Self-supervised pretraining partly mitigates the domain gap by learning modality-aware features directly from medical data, complementing conventional transfer pipelines [4].

Given annotation bottlenecks, learning paradigms beyond full supervision are increasingly important. Semi-supervised approaches exploit unlabeled data through consistency regularization and teacher-student ensembling; relation-driven self-ensembling further leverages inter-sample structure to improve medical image classification [5]. Weak supervision relaxes pixel- or voxel-level labeling requirements, enabling segmentation from extreme points [6], registration from anatomical correspondences rather than dense deformations [7], and image-level classification under multiple-instance assumptions [8]. Collectively, these paradigms indicate a broader shift in medical imaging from purely label-intensive supervision toward representation-centric learning that better matches clinical data realities.

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Medical Imaging Modalities
subsections.subsection_title: Medical Imaging Applications and Emerging Robustness Directions
subsections.content:
Deep learning now supports a wide spectrum of medical imaging applications beyond canonical diagnosis-oriented classification, including dynamic motion analysis, cross-modality synthesis, and image restoration. In cardiac MRI, joint models that couple motion estimation with segmentation illustrate how task synergy can improve both anatomical delineation and functional characterization, especially when annotations are temporally sparse ref [20]. In ophthalmic imaging, transfer-learning-based DenseNet variants have likewise shown practical utility for fundus image classification under limited labeled data, reflecting a common clinical setting in screening workflows ref [10].

A second application axis concerns image enhancement and modality transformation. Image synthesis networks can infer clinically useful contrasts or surrogate modalities from available scans, potentially reducing acquisition burden and expanding downstream analysis options; residual encoder-decoder designs have reported gains for medical image synthesis across mammography and neuroimaging settings ref [9]. Likewise, artifact-focused restoration has become increasingly important for CT, where metal artifacts can obscure anatomy and compromise diagnosis. Unsupervised disentanglement strategies are especially appealing because they avoid reliance on imperfect synthetic corruption models and may generalize better to real clinical data ref [22].

Alongside these advances, robustness is emerging as a central translational requirement. Medical AI systems can fail under distribution shift, acquisition artifacts, annotation sparsity, or even adversarial perturbations; the latter have been extensively documented in computer vision and are increasingly recognized as a relevant safety concern for medical imaging pipelines ref [19]. Promising directions therefore include artifact-aware learning, multi-task consistency constraints, uncertainty estimation, and robustness evaluation under realistic perturbation and domain-shift settings, so that high benchmark accuracy translates into dependable clinical performance ref [20], ref [22], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Analytical Applications in Medical Imaging
subsections.content:
Deep learning has become an important alternative to hand-crafted and optimization-heavy pipelines for image registration. In deformable registration, unsupervised feature learning was used to derive compact hierarchical patch descriptors that improved anatomical correspondence estimation and generalized across datasets and even new 7T MRI acquisitions, reducing reliance on manually engineered similarity measures ref [24]. For interventional alignment, CNN-based regression further shifted 2D/3D registration from iterative similarity maximization to direct pose estimation, enabling real-time performance with enlarged capture range in fluoroscopy-guided applications ref [25]. These studies exemplify a broader transition from metric design to representation learning and parameter regression.

In reconstruction and enhancement, deep networks have been especially influential in low-dose imaging. Projection- or image-domain CNNs were shown to suppress noise while preserving structural detail in low-dose CT ref [27], and related tomography work demonstrated that learned enhancement of low-exposure X-ray projections can substantially recover signal-to-noise ratio and improve downstream 3D reconstruction quality in radiation-sensitive settings ref [26]. Beyond CT, deep models have also been adapted to dynamic PET, where stacked sparse autoencoder-based reconstruction exploited spatial-temporal dependencies across frames to reduce noise and better preserve lesion boundaries than conventional framewise reconstruction ref [28].

A common theme across registration, reconstruction, and enhancement is that deep networks embed stronger priors on anatomy, physics, and inter-frame consistency than classical handcrafted models. Nevertheless, robustness across scanners, doses, and anatomies remains a central concern, and many early methods relied on synthetic pairs or limited training regimes ref [25], ref [27], ref [28]. Current survey evidence therefore suggests that the main clinical promise of these approaches lies not only in quality gains, but also in faster workflows, reduced radiation burden, and improved compatibility with time-sensitive image-guided procedures ref [25], ref [26], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Analytical Applications in Medical Imaging
subsections.subsection_title: Radiomics, Staging, Prognosis, and Clinical Outcome Prediction
subsections.content:
Radiomics has evolved from handcrafted, high-throughput image descriptors to deep feature learning, enabling noninvasive estimation of tumor biology, disease stage, and outcome. In breast imaging, MR radiomic phenotypes have shown associations with receptor status and intrinsic molecular subtypes, supporting the broader radiogenomic premise that imaging can serve as a surrogate for clinically meaningful biology ref [29], ref [30]. Similar links have been reported for recurrence risk, where MR radiomics correlated with research versions of MammaPrint, Oncotype DX, and PAM50, with tumor size and enhancement heterogeneity emerging as recurrent prognostic markers ref [31]. Deep feature-based radiomics has further extended this paradigm in glioblastoma, where transfer learning-derived MRI signatures improved survival stratification beyond traditional clinical factors ref [33].

Deep learning has also been used more directly for disease staging. In chest CT, CNNs trained on smokers distinguished COPD, approximated GOLD stage, and predicted acute respiratory events and mortality, while retaining reasonable transportability from COPDGene to ECLIPSE ref [32]. In ophthalmology, deep learning improved diabetic retinopathy staging by inferring severity from limited-field fundus photographs and even approximating prognosis-oriented grading, illustrating how data-driven models can capture latent contextual cues beyond explicit human criteria ref [35]. At the histopathology scale, survival after hepatocellular carcinoma resection has been predicted from whole-slide images using weakly supervised attention-based models, with prognostic regions enriched for vascular spaces, macrotrabecular architecture, and reduced immune infiltration ref [8].

Across applications, the main promise is individualized risk estimation for treatment selection, surveillance intensity, and trial stratification; however, the main bottlenecks remain unchanged: small and imbalanced cohorts, limited external validation, endpoint heterogeneity, and insufficient interpretability. Even studies integrating radiomics and genomics reported only modest gains over single-modality predictors in small cohorts ref [30], and several prognostic models remain vulnerable to acquisition shift and selection bias ref [32], ref [33]. Future survey directions therefore emphasize multimodal fusion, calibrated survival modeling, pathology-imaging-genomics integration, and rigorous multi-center validation before these systems can be relied upon for routine staging and outcome prediction.

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Analytical Applications in Medical Imaging
subsections.content:
Segmentation, detection, and anatomical localization are among the most mature clinical uses of deep learning in medical imaging, but they impose different geometric demands. For pixel- and voxel-wise delineation, encoder-decoder architectures with skip connections became foundational because they jointly preserve context and boundary detail, as exemplified by U-Net for 2D biomedical segmentation and V-Net for end-to-end volumetric prediction with Dice-based optimization in 3D MRI ref [10], ref [37]. These models helped shift practice away from patch-wise classification toward dense prediction, while also motivating task-specific losses and extensive augmentation for limited annotations ref [10], ref [37].

Application-specific systems then demonstrated how these principles transfer to difficult organs and lesions. DeepOrgan combined coarse candidate generation with multi-level ConvNets for pancreas segmentation, highlighting the utility of coarse-to-fine region refinement in anatomically variable abdominal CT ref [8]. Similar ideas were used for liver tumor delineation in CT, where deep CNNs improved automatic lesion segmentation despite low contrast and heterogeneous appearance ref [38]. Beyond segmentation, deep models also strengthened biomarker detection: 3D CNNs enabled sensitive cerebral microbleed detection from MR volumes by exploiting full spatial context, and related tracking-based frameworks used learned vessel representations to recover connected vascular trees rather than isolated responses ref [40], ref [9].

Anatomical localization has likewise benefited from learned spatial features. CNN-based distal femur landmark detection showed that deep models can estimate clinically meaningful landmarks by combining image evidence with downstream geometric constraints on the recovered surface ref [39]. More broadly, these studies reveal a common trend: successful systems increasingly couple deep appearance modeling with structural priors, cascaded candidate refinement, or topology-aware post-processing, especially when targets are small, elongated, or weakly contrasted ref [39], ref [40], ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Analytical Applications in Medical Imaging
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations, Datasets, and Survey Perspectives in Medical Imaging AI
subsections.content:
Foundations in medical imaging AI are rooted in earlier computer-aided detection and quantitative image analysis, where segmentation, feature extraction, classifier design, and observer evaluation were already formalized as core components of image-based decision support ref [45]. This historical lineage is important because current deep learning systems inherit many of the same concerns—image quality, annotation validity, robustness, and clinically meaningful evaluation—while operating at a much larger representational scale ref [45], ref [12].

Recent survey perspectives emphasize that medical imaging AI is shaped as much by data constraints as by model design. Broad reviews identify limited annotation, domain shift, class imbalance, interpretability, and regulatory translation as persistent bottlenecks, with dataset scarcity emerging as the dominant cross-cutting challenge ref [12], ref [43]. Textural analysis remains conceptually relevant in this context: classical descriptors such as co-occurrence-based texture features helped establish quantitative image phenotyping and continue to inform radiomics and representation learning pipelines ref [14].

Dataset-oriented position papers further argue that useful machine learning corpora must be not only large, but also well curated, interoperable, and reusable. Key requirements include reliable ground truth, standardized metadata, de-identification, provenance tracking, and explicit train/validation/test partitioning, ideally aligned with FAIR principles and regulatory needs ref [10], ref [11]. Practical data preparation therefore spans ethics approval, query and retrieval from PACS, DICOM de-identification, harmonization, annotation, and external validation, all of which materially affect downstream performance and generalizability ref [11], ref [10].

From a survey standpoint, the field is also becoming increasingly specialized: task-focused reviews, such as those on semantic segmentation, provide useful taxonomies of architectures, supervision regimes, losses, and dataset practices, thereby clarifying where progress reflects genuine methodological advances versus benchmark-specific optimization ref [43]. Looking forward, progress in medical imaging AI will depend less on marginal architectural novelty alone and more on shared datasets, reproducible curation workflows, and evaluation standards that connect algorithmic performance to clinical utility ref [12], ref [10], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Analytical Applications in Medical Imaging
subsections.content:
Image classification and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) remain among the most mature clinical uses of deep learning in medical imaging, where convolutional architectures increasingly replace hand-crafted pipelines by learning disease-discriminative representations directly from pixels. Across pathology, ophthalmology, thoracic imaging, and breast imaging, recent studies show that end-to-end models, transfer learning, and feature-fusion strategies can substantially improve diagnostic sensitivity and specificity relative to conventional feature engineering ref [48], ref [49], ref [52], ref [12].

In histopathology, deep networks have been used for early breast cancer recognition from digitized tissue images, demonstrating the suitability of learned multiscale texture and morphology cues for malignancy classification ref [48]. More generally, hybrid schemes that combine deep features with statistical descriptors and classify them using multilayer perceptrons indicate that fused representations can outperform either feature family alone, especially when datasets are moderate in size ref [49]. During the COVID-19 pandemic, CNN-based CAD systems such as PAM-DenseNet further highlighted the value of densely connected architectures for rapid thoracic image triage, although concerns about dataset bias and clinical generalizability remain important ref [50].

Ophthalmic and breast imaging provide some of the clearest evidence of clinical utility. Deep ensembles and integrated learning strategies have improved automated diabetic retinopathy detection on public fundus datasets ref [52], while transfer learning has been effective for digital mammographic tumor classification ref [12]. Breast MRI maximum-intensity projections have also been exploited to simplify 3D data into diagnostically informative views for lesion classification with CNNs ref [54]. Beyond lesion diagnosis, deep models are increasingly used for risk stratification, as shown in mammography-based breast cancer risk assessment and in multimodal or cross-feature fusion frameworks for breast cancer diagnosis ref [14], ref [13]. Collectively, these studies suggest that future CAD systems will depend less on isolated classifiers and more on robust multimodal learning, calibration, and prospective validation across institutions ref [54], ref [13], ref [14].

Evaluation of deep-learning-based segmentation in medical imaging is dominated by overlap and boundary criteria. The Dice similarity coefficient remains the most frequently reported metric because it directly quantifies spatial agreement between predicted and reference masks and is particularly interpretable for class-wise tissue and lesion segmentation in MRI ref [56], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. Closely related overlap measures such as the Jaccard index are often reported for completeness, while pixel- or voxel-level sensitivity, specificity, precision, and volumetric similarity are useful for characterizing class imbalance and under- versus over-segmentation behavior ref [5], ref [6].

Because overlap scores can obscure boundary defects, many studies complement Dice with distance-based metrics, especially the Hausdorff distance and average symmetric surface distance, which better capture clinically relevant contour deviations for organs and lesions ref [5], ref [7], ref [8]. For highly imbalanced detection tasks, including microbleeds or small focal lesions, free-response receiver operating characteristic analysis, lesion-wise sensitivity, false positives per case, and average precision are often more informative than voxel overlap alone ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. Detection studies also frequently summarize discrimination using ROC curves and area under the curve, but lesion-level localization metrics should accompany these global scores when spatial correctness is central ref [10], ref [12].

Metric choice should also reflect the training and annotation setting. In brain MRI segmentation, adversarially trained and dilated CNNs have been evaluated not only with Dice but also with structural indicators such as the number of connected components, highlighting that anatomically plausible outputs may improve even when Dice gains are modest ref [2]. More broadly, challenge-style evaluations increasingly recommend reporting multiple complementary metrics, class-wise distributions, and statistical significance testing across cases to avoid overinterpreting single-number improvements ref [7], ref [13], ref [14]. In MRI applications, this multidimensional evaluation is particularly important because small lesions, fuzzy boundaries, and inter-rater variability can strongly affect apparent model performance ref [3], ref [8], ref [15], ref [16].

subsections.subsection_title: General Evaluation Frameworks in MRI Deep Learning
subsections.content:
General evaluation in MRI deep learning extends beyond task-specific scores to an end-to-end assessment of the full pipeline, including data curation, preprocessing, model development, internal validation, and external testing. A standard supervised workflow separates training, validation, and test sets to estimate generalization, but MRI studies additionally require attention to scanner heterogeneity, sequence-dependent contrast, and institution-specific acquisition biases. Broad reviews of MRI-oriented deep learning consistently emphasize that methodological rigor in split design and testing protocol is as important as architectural novelty ref [57], ref [2], ref [3].

A robust framework should therefore combine several complementary evaluation layers. First, technical validation measures predictive accuracy under fixed experimental conditions, often with cross-validation or held-out testing; second, generalization analysis evaluates performance across sites, vendors, protocols, and patient subgroups; third, reproducibility analysis examines sensitivity to preprocessing, random initialization, and annotation variability. Public datasets, challenge benchmarks, and open implementations have become central to this process because they improve comparability and facilitate external replication ref [57], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6].

For MRI, clinically meaningful evaluation also requires calibration to downstream use. Reconstruction and restoration models are often assessed with image fidelity metrics, yet these should be complemented by reader studies or downstream task performance; similarly, registration and segmentation systems should be evaluated not only numerically but also for anatomical plausibility, failure modes, and uncertainty behavior ref [57], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. Recent reviews further argue for reporting uncertainty, interpretability, robustness to distribution shift, and workflow integration, especially because MRI models may fail when deployed outside the narrow distribution represented in research cohorts ref [10], ref [11], ref [12].

Accordingly, a practical general evaluation framework in MRI deep learning should report dataset provenance, split strategy at the patient level, preprocessing details, internal and external validation, confidence intervals, ablation studies, and, where possible, prospective or multicenter testing. Such reporting helps distinguish true clinical utility from optimistic laboratory performance and remains a prerequisite for trustworthy translation of MRI deep learning systems into practice ref [57], ref [2], ref [3], ref [10], ref [13].

Figures and tables in surveys on deep learning for medical imaging should do more than summarize results; they should expose the field’s methodological structure. A useful figure typically maps the pipeline from data acquisition and preprocessing to representation learning, task-specific prediction, and clinical deployment, while distinguishing major tasks such as classification, detection, segmentation, registration, reconstruction, and prognosis modeling ref [46], ref [5], ref [42], ref [43]. Timeline figures are also valuable for showing the transition from early deep belief networks and patch-based CNNs to fully convolutional, residual, and self-/transfer-learning paradigms ref [3], ref [2], ref [9], ref [16].

Comparative tables should be organized by imaging modality, task, supervision level, dataset scale, and evaluation metrics rather than by model name alone. For segmentation, representative entries often include volumetric and encoder-decoder designs such as V-Net, DeepOrgan, and adversarial or weakly supervised formulations ref [36], ref [40], ref [56], ref [13]. For reconstruction, synthesis, and image enhancement, tables should separately identify low-dose restoration, PET reconstruction, and cross-modality synthesis because these problems differ in physics constraints and target metrics ref [27], ref [28], ref [22], ref [26].

To improve interpretability, tables should additionally report annotation burden, external validation, and clinical endpoint relevance. Studies on diabetic retinopathy grading, mammography risk assessment, histopathology prognosis, and CT-based disease staging illustrate how task success depends not only on architecture, but also on cohort composition, labeling protocol, and outcome definition ref [34], ref [55], ref [35], ref [32]. In a holistic survey, well-designed figures and tables therefore function as analytical instruments that reveal trends, gaps, and opportunities across the medical imaging workflow.
